newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa drug industry warns of disinvestment.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa drug industry warns of disinvestment.

text.p: South Africa's pharmaceutical manufacturer's industry on Thursday warned that foreign firms may disinvest from South Africa if planned health reforms go ahead.
Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma earlier unveiled the final changes to planned legislation that is seeking to cut the cost of the country's health burden.
But a senior drug industry figure said the changes were not enough, though she added final judgement would be reserved until the full wording of the planned laws is released.
"South Africa is still saying you (the overseas drugs industry) are not welcome here," Mirryena Deeb, chief executive of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers' Association, told Reuters.

The changes did scrap plans to limit the use of brand names by firms selling to the state, but have kept legislation substituting branded drugs with cheaper generic equivalents and "parallel importing" of drugs.

Zuma says parallel imports are necessary because some drugs are far more expensive in South Africa than they in other countries. Currently, drugs that are registered by a South African manufacturer are bought from that manufacturer. Under the new system, the South African government would buy a drug in another country if it was cheaper there.

Deeb said the industry did not totally oppose parallel imports as long as drugs brought in were as tightly checked for safety as local products and also had to undergo the same registration process -- with attendant costs.
The drugs industry says it is also willing to fight generics, which are versions of off-patent branded drugs, on a level commercial playing field, but that Zuma's plans make their use mandatory.
"We have said time and time again we don't mind fair competition," Deeb said.

The latest changes to the plans are the second time Zuma has sought to make concessions to the drugs industry after she backed down last year in the face of a legal challenge from SmithKline Beecham Plc.
The laws, which have a stamp of approval from South Africa's cabinet, will now go to parliament to be discussed.

Deeb, fresh from a European trip to meet overseas drug industry executives, said it was not clear if there would be another legal challenge to Zuma. She added she feared overseas firms may simply cancel investment in the country or start to pull out.

"There is a concern from the international pharmaceuticals community about the commitment of South Africa to market principles and my great fear is that they may not bother with a legal challenge and will just leave. It could be a tragedy," she said.
Several leading drug firms have warned that South Africa's policies could threaten future investment from the industry, including the world's biggest drugs firm Glaxo Wellcome Plc.
